content: Glechoma hederacea, commonly known as Ground-ivy, is a perennial, aromatic, evergreen creeping plant belonging to the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is native to Europe and southwestern Asia but has been introduced to North America, where it is now widespread except in the Rocky Mountains. This plant is also referred to by various names, including Alehoof, Creeping Charlie, Catsfoot (due to the shape and size of its leaves), Field Balm, Run-away-robin, Gill-over-the-ground, and Tunhoof. Occasionally, it is called Creeping Jenny, though this name more commonly applies to Lysimachia nummularia. The plant is characterized by its round to kidney-shaped (reniform) leaves with crenate (rounded-toothed) edges. These leaves are 2–3 cm in diameter and are attached to square stems via petioles that are 3–6 cm long. The stems root at the nodes, allowing the plant to spread. Glechoma hederacea is a variable species, with its size ranging from 5 cm to 50 cm depending on environmental conditions. It is sometimes mistaken for common mallow (Malva neglecta), which also has round, lobed leaves. However, mallow leaves attach to the stem at the back of the leaf, whereas Ground-ivy leaves attach at the center. Additionally, Ground-ivy has square stems, more prominent rounded lobes on its leaf edges, and a hairy upper leaf surface. Unlike mallow and other creeping plants, Ground-ivy spreads from nodes on its stems. When damaged, it emits a distinctive odor, a characteristic of plants in the mint family. The flowers of Glechoma hederacea are bilaterally symmetrical, funnel-shaped, and range in color from blue or bluish-violet to lavender. They grow in clusters of two or three in the leaf axils on the upper part of the stem or near the tip. The plant typically flowers in the spring. It thrives in moist, shaded areas but can also tolerate full sun. It is commonly found in grasslands, wooded areas, wastelands, lawns, and around buildings, as it can survive mowing. The plant spreads through stolons or seeds, with its rhizomatous reproduction contributing to its wide distribution. It often forms dense mats that can dominate lawns, making it an invasive or aggressive weed. Ecological Aspects Ground-ivy is visited by various wild bees, including species such as Anthophora furcata, Anthidium manicatum, Anthophora plumipes, Anthophora quadrimaculata, Osmia aurulenta, Osmia caerulentes, and Osmia uncinata. Cultivation and Uses Glechoma hederacea is sometimes cultivated as a potted plant or ground cover. A variegated variety is occasionally available commercially. While often considered a weed due to its invasive nature, the plant has culinary and medicinal uses, which were the reasons for its introduction to America by early European settlers. The fresh herb can be rinsed and steeped in hot water to make an herbal tea rich in vitamin C. The plant’s essential oil possesses potent medicinal properties. Historically, it has been used as a general tonic for colds and coughs and to relieve congestion of the mucous membranes. It also exhibits anti-inflammatory properties and has been claimed to promote the excretion of lead in urine. The medicinal properties of Glechoma hederacea have been recognized for centuries. Galen, the ancient physician, recommended it for treating eye inflammation. John Gerard, an English herbalist, suggested its use for tinnitus and described it as a diuretic, astringent, tonic, and gentle stimulant. He also noted its utility in kidney diseases, indigestion, and as a lung herb. The Saxons widely used the plant in brewing beer as a flavoring, clarifying, and preservative agent before the introduction of hops, which explains its brewing-related names such as Alehoof, Tunhoof, and Gill-over-the-ground. Control Glechoma hederacea is often regarded as a weed, a characteristic it shares with many other members of the mint family. It thrives in heavy, fertile soils with high moisture and low boron content. It is particularly problematic in shady areas where grass struggles to grow, though it can also be an issue in full sun. Small infestations can be managed through hand weeding, but repeated efforts are necessary due to the plant’s rhizomatous nature, which allows it to regrow from roots or stem fragments. The plant is unusually sensitive to boron and can be controlled by applying a solution of sodium tetraborate (borax). However, boron is toxic to other plants and animals at slightly higher concentrations and does not break down in the environment. Therefore, the long-term effects of boron application on soil and groundwater are likely unfavorable. Aside from mechanical removal or borax treatment, commercial herbicides can be used to manage Glechoma infestations. There is some disagreement about the effectiveness of various herbicides, with dicamba (found in products like Trimec and Weed-B-Gon) and 2,4-D being described as both effective and ineffective by different sources. This variability may be due to differences in subpopulations of the plant, application rates, or timing. To prevent herbicide resistance, it is recommended to rotate products rather than using the same one repeatedly. Triclopyr has been reported as effective, while clopyralid, MCPP, and quinclorac are considered ineffective. Fluroxypyr and Confront have also been described as effective, but their sale is restricted to professionals. Two applications, spaced 10–14 days apart, are typically necessary. Surviving plants may regenerate after 24 days, requiring additional treatments four to five weeks later and possibly further follow-ups. The timing of herbicide application is also critical; fall is generally the best time for broadleaf herbicides, though slow-acting herbicides like triclopyr may not show results until the next growing season. Other effective techniques include fertilizing with more than two pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet annually and using the preemergence herbicide isoxaben. In extreme cases, a short-lived full-spectrum herbicide like Roundup may be used to kill the entire lawn, which is then reseeded from scratch.
